title: Bread with salt (Avot 6:4)
hook: the way of Torah: bread with salt, water by measure, a simple bed
tomorrow: forty-eight ways to get Torah. why so many more than a crown?

segments.voice: Yesterday: even one letter. Learn a single letter from someone and you owe them honor. Now the last pages of Avot ask a plainer question: what does a learner actually need?
screen: `EVEN ONE LETTER.` → `WHAT DOES A LEARNER NEED?`

segments.voice: Three cardboard boxes on a kitchen floor, labeled in marker: keep, give, toss. The give box is overflowing. The keep box holds a kettle, one pot, a bread knife and a salt shaker shaped like a lighthouse. A granddaughter holds up a stand mixer. Seriously? Her grandfather shrugs. Bread with salt, he says. That's what the sages said a learner needs. She's sure he's being dramatic. So what did the sages actually say?
screen: `KEEP. GIVE. TOSS.` → `ONE POT, ONE KETTLE.` → `WHAT DID THE SAGES SAY?`

segments.voice: The sixth chapter of Pirkei Avot says it bluntly. This is the way of Torah: eat bread with salt, drink water by measure, sleep on the ground, live a life of hardship, and toil in Torah. Then it makes a promise, borrowing a line from Psalms: "happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee." Happy in this world, the Mishnah explains, and well with you in the world to come. Read fast, it sounds like a vow of poverty. Some classic commentators read it another way: as a floor, not a rule. Even if bread with salt is all you have, don't stop learning. Nothing here tells anyone to throw out the mixer. It says the learning doesn't wait for the kitchen to be perfect. That's the turn. The list isn't about how little you own. It's about how little you need before you start. Water by measure and a hard bed aren't prizes, and they aren't punishments either. They're the worst case, named out loud, with Torah still on the table. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this saying, the promise of happiness doesn't wait for comfort. It sits right next to the bread and the salt. Back on the kitchen floor, the grandfather isn't giving up his life. He's checking what it was resting on all along. A kettle. A pot. A book. Enough.
screen: `THE WAY OF TORAH: BREAD WITH SALT.` · `HAPPY SHALT THOU BE.` · `A FLOOR, NOT A RULE.` · `THE LEARNING DOESN'T WAIT.` · then, large: `BREAD WITH SALT.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in and choose three things you'd keep if you had one small box: something to eat from, something to learn from, and something that's simply yours. Rest your eyes on them, or hold them if they're near, for the whole sit. Notice that the list fits.
Bread with salt. Avot's picture of the bare minimum, and its promise that the learning can start right there.
Keep this one: bread with salt, enough to start on. Just two more days of Avot.

howItsDone: Many communities keep a custom of reading a chapter of Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the spring and summer, and its sixth chapter, on acquiring Torah, is part of that cycle.

fork.setup: your friend wants to learn guitar but says she'll wait until she can afford a good one. what does Avot 6:4 point to?
options: start on the borrowed one; the learning doesn't wait for the perfect setup.
wait; doing it properly means having the right tools first.
sell what she owns first, since the way of Torah means owning nothing.
fork.reveal: the saying names the bare minimum and puts the learning right on top of it. it doesn't ask anyone to get rid of things; it asks them not to wait.

original.note: Hebrew: bread with salt you shall eat, the first step on Avot's way of Torah.

chat.says: saba is giving away his WHOLE kitchen. says he needs 'bread with salt.' is that even a real thing??
options: It's Avot 6:4. Not a vow of poverty: the learning doesn't wait for a full kitchen.
It's Avot 6:4. Real learners are supposed to own almost nothing at all.
It's about welcome: always keep bread and salt ready for any guest.
chat.meaning: Avot's way of Torah names the bare minimum, bread with salt, and says the learning and the happiness can start right there.
